The relation between these lines and the rest of the draft is impossible to determine con-
fidently, but S. evidently left them undeveloped as being out of harmony with the more
generalised plangency of the three stanzas. For her part, Mary did not append this frag-
ment, possibly intended for a further stanza, to any of her published texts — so excluding
an element of personal conflict, even betrayal, which figured in the original conception of
the poem.
 The unusual stanza of five eight-syllable lines rhyming aabbb is that of Misery. —
A Fragment (Longman ii, no. 202), though that poem employs a seven-syllable line vary-
ing to eight. Besides the common theme of the cessation of both erotic passion and love,
the two poems exhibit a number of verbal similarities; see, for example, the note to ll. 8–9.
 Indeed, When passion’s trance might seem to take up Misery’s rhetorical supposition ‘If
love can live when pleasure dies’ (l. 18) in order to offer a negative response structured
